vignette:
She was twenty-three, a newly qualified midwife in a busy hospital in her hometown. She loved the rhythm of the labour ward-the controlled chaos, the cries, the relief after a safe delivery. One night after a long shift, a male colleague she trusted offered her a ride home. Instead, he drove to a secluded area and raped her. She remembers the way the car door handle felt cold against her palm as she tried to open it. She remembers the smell of his aftershave, cloying and sweet, mixing with the metallic taste of blood in her mouth. She did not scream. She did not tell anyone. She went home, showered, and went to work the next day.

For years she buried it. She threw herself into her work, delivering babies with fierce competence. She married a kind man who worked in construction, and they had two children. She never connected the dots. But the body remembers.

Now she is fifty-seven, still a midwife in a community clinic. Every birth brings a shadow. When a woman is in transition, screaming, her legs in stirrups, the patient's vulnerability and the sterile scent of antiseptic and latex wash over her, and she is back in that car. Her hands tremble as she guides the baby's shoulders. Sometimes she has to step out of the room, pretending she needs more gauze. She stands in the supply closet, heart hammering, counting the seconds until she can return.

She avoids night shifts now. She cannot bear the dark parking lot, even though the clinic is well-lit. She takes the bus, even when her husband offers to drive her. The bus is safer because she can sit near the driver. She cannot sit with her back to the door in any room. At dinner with friends, she always chooses the seat against the wall.

At home, she is brittle. Her husband reaches for her in bed, and she freezes. Sometimes she lets him touch her, but her mind goes elsewhere-to a checklist of medications needed for a preeclamptic patient, to the colour of the tiles in the labour ward. He has stopped reaching. She feels guilty, but not guilty enough to force herself.

She has not told him about the rape. She told no one until last month, when she walked into a therapist's office because she could no longer sleep. The nightmares are vivid: in them, she is on the delivery table, legs spread, and the colleague is the doctor, and no one helps her. She wakes up drenched in sweat, gasping, her husband stirring beside her. She lies still until dawn.

She is hypervigilant in the clinic. When a male doctor walks behind her, she flinches. When a patient's husband raises his voice in the waiting room, her throat closes. She checks the locks on the medication cabinet three times before leaving. She has started writing the same checklist on her palm, as if her mind cannot hold onto small facts.

Her colleagues notice she is quieter. She used to laugh easily. Now she watches the clock. She feels a constant low hum of dread, like a machine running in her chest. She is still good at her job-the mothers trust her-but the work costs her more than it gives.

Sometimes, after a difficult birth, she goes to the bathroom and cries. Not for the mother, but for the girl who never told. She thinks: I should have said something. I should have screamed. But she didn't. And now the silence has a weight of its own, pressing down on her chest as she walks home, alone, every evening, watching the rearview mirror for headlights that are not there.
